content: Our six-person home-storage brand sells through a hosted ecommerce storefront. Monthly revenue is $120,000 from 1,500 orders at an $80 average order value. Of those orders, 600 are first orders acquired through $18,000 in paid advertising, so our paid customer acquisition cost is $30; the other 900 are repeat orders. Gross margin after product cost is 60%. Shipping, fulfillment, and payment fees cost another $8 per order. Existing fixed operating costs, including all six salaries, are $36,000 per month. We have $32,000 in cash and no debt. I handle marketing as the founder, but it takes 15 hours a week and I can spare only four. We can hire an in-house marketer at $58,000 a year plus 20% for employer taxes and benefits, with a one-time $2,000 recruiting cost, or retain an agency for $4,500 a month plus $1,500 onboarding. Advertising spend stays at $18,000 under either option. The employee could start in six weeks and own email, ads, and creative; the agency can start next week on a three-month minimum contract but only handles ads, leaving email and creative with me. Neither promises sales growth. Which option, if either, should we choose? Show current monthly operating surplus, each option's recurring and upfront costs, and the extra monthly orders needed to cover the recurring cost at current unit economics with advertising spend held flat. Propose a 90-day decision plan that accounts for cash, ramp time, and the work still on my plate. State assumptions rather than treating repeat purchases or growth as guaranteed.

# Recommendation: Hire the in-house marketer, with a cash floor and clear checkpoints

Your real problem is capacity. Marketing needs about 15 hours a week, and you can give only 4. Only the employee closes that gap. The agency costs less per month but covers only ads, so you would still be short on email and creative work.

Either option uses up most of your current surplus, so neither is low-risk.

## 1. Current monthly operating surplus

| Line | Monthly |
|---|---|
| Revenue (1,500 × $80) | $120,000 |
| Gross profit (60%) | $72,000 |
| Shipping, fulfillment, payment ($8 × 1,500) | –$12,000 |
| Paid advertising | –$18,000 |
| Fixed operating costs | –$36,000 |
| **Operating surplus** | **$6,000** |

Unit economics:
- **Contribution per order:** $80 × 60% – $8 = **$40**
- **First paid order:** $40 – $30 CAC = **$10** profit
- **Repeat order:** $40, if it needs no extra paid spend

## 2. Option costs and break-even

| | In-house marketer | Agency |
|---|---|---|
| Recurring monthly cost | $58,000 × 1.2 ÷ 12 = **$5,800** | **$4,500** |
| Upfront cost | **$2,000** recruiting | **$1,500** onboarding |
| Minimum commitment | None beyond notice or severance norms | 3 months = $13,500 + $1,500 = **$15,000** |
| Start | About week 6 | Next week |
| Covers | Email, ads, creative | Ads only |
| Surplus if no growth | **$200/month** | **$1,500/month** |
| Extra orders to cover recurring cost ($40 each) | 5,800 ÷ 40 = **145/month** (+9.7%) | 4,500 ÷ 40 = **113/month** (+7.5%) |
| Revenue needed for those orders | about $11,600 | about $9,000 |

Advertising stays at $18,000, so those extra orders must come from one of three sources:
- **Better ad efficiency.** If all the extra orders came from ads alone, CAC would need to fall to about **$24.16** for the employee (745 first orders) or **$25.25** for the agency (713 first orders).
- **More repeat orders** from email and retention.
- **Higher conversion** or **higher order value.**

Only the employee works on all three of these. The agency can only move ad efficiency.

## 3. Cash over the first 90 days

These figures assume the $6,000 surplus holds.

| | Employee | Agency |
|---|---|---|
| Upfront cost | $2,000 | $1,500 |
| Salary or fees in first 90 days | about 1.5 months × $5,800 ≈ $8,700 | $13,500 |
| **Total 90-day outlay** | **≈ $10,700** | **$15,000** |
| 90-day surplus ($18,000) minus outlay | +$7,300 | +$3,000 |
| Cash at day 90 | ≈ $39,300 | ≈ $35,000 |

The downside matters more:
- **If orders fall 10%** (150 orders × $40 = $6,000), your surplus drops to zero.
- **With the employee in place,** you would then lose about $5,800 a month. Your $32,000 covers about **5.5 months**.
- **With the agency,** you would lose $4,500 a month and are locked in for 3 months.

## 4. Why the employee, and when to pick something else

**Choose the employee because:**
- **It covers your hour gap.** I've assumed your 15 hours split roughly 6 on ads and 9 on email and creative. The agency would then leave you about 9 hours of work against 4 spare, still a 5-hour weekly shortfall. The employee covers all 15.
- **Email is your cheapest lever.** Repeat orders earn $40 with no CAC. A modest lift in repeat purchases could deliver much of the 145 orders.
- **It's cheaper in the first 90 days** and has no three-month lock-in.

**Choose the agency instead only if** ads are clearly your main weakness (CAC rising, poor creative testing) and email and creative are already in good shape on 4 hours a week.

**Choose neither if** cash is needed elsewhere, such as an inventory buy. In that case, simplify: run automated email flows only and keep ads at their current settings.

## 5. 90-day decision plan

**Days 1–14: baseline and setup**
- Lock in baseline metrics: weekly orders, first vs. repeat split, CAC, conversion rate, average order value, and email revenue.
- Set a **cash floor of $20,000**. If cash approaches it, pause any new spending.
- Post the role. Hire for a generalist who has run Shopify-style email flows and paid social campaigns.
- Spend your 4 hours on two things only: keeping ads stable and running the existing email automations. Drop or pause all other creative work.

**Days 15–42: recruiting**
- Hire by about week 6.
- Write a 30/60/90-day scorecard before they start:
  - **Day 30:** audit done, email flows fixed (welcome, post-purchase, win-back).
  - **Day 60:** a regular creative testing cadence running.
  - **Day 90:** a measurable trend toward +145 orders a month.
- **Fallback:** if no strong candidate appears by day 35, consider a 1–2 month freelancer for ads with no minimum commitment. Don't sign the 3-month agency contract just to fill the gap.

**Days 43–90: ramp**
- Track leading indicators weekly: CAC, repeat rate, and email revenue share.
- Don't expect break-even yet. The hire will be only about 7 weeks in.

**Day 90 review**
- **On track:** extra orders running at 75 or more a month, or CAC under about $27 → continue.
- **Flat with cash above $25,000:** set explicit day-150 targets and continue.
- **Declining or cash near the $20,000 floor:** restructure the role or end it.

## Assumptions to check

- **The $6,000 surplus is not cash in the bank.** It ignores inventory purchases, taxes, and any owner draw. Check your inventory cash cycle in particular.
- **Repeat orders are not guaranteed.** I've assumed the 900 repeat orders keep coming at a similar rate. If the repeat rate is slipping because email is neglected, your baseline is overstated.
- **No sales growth is promised by either option.** Break-even depends entirely on the 113–145 extra orders a month actually appearing.
- **CAC may change.** CAC stays at $30 only if ad performance holds, and it could rise during the transition.
